newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Pressure on Russian Norilsk heats up.
newsitem.headline: Pressure on Russian Norilsk heats up.

text.p: Pressure on Russia's giant Norilsk Nickel metals group to get its financial act together mounted on Wednesday, with parliament calling for state aid and delivering a blistering attack on the firm's restructuring plans.
But RAO Norilsky Nickel announced a major survival plan and said it would boost metals production and increase efficiency into the next millenium.

The scrambling over what Norilsk -- one of the world's key suppliers of nickel, cobalt, platinum, palladium and other platinum group metals -- needs to survive came on the eve of a deadline set by Norilsk workers upset over wage arrears.

Labourers in the remote and inhospitable Arctic town of Norilsk, where the company's flagship plant is based, have given management through Thursday to come up with a plan to pay off overdue salaries and increase future wages.

The State Duma lower parliament house, seeking to ram its own plan for Norilsk through the government, overwhelmingly approved a non-binding proposal asking the cabinet to support the company and extend state control over its shares.
The Duma proposals also called for blocking Norilsk restructuring plans by commercial bank Uneximbank, which has a 38 percent stake in Norilsk, or 51 percent of voting shares.
Duma deputies said Uneximbank's plans to restructure the giant by breaking it up were "inadmissable".

"This would lead to the break-up of the single technological structure...and to the loss of the government's right to regulate and control output of nickel and copper ore and platinum group metals," the Duma proposal said.
Shortly before the Duma vote, Norilsk announced bold but scantily-clad plans to boost production of nickel, copper and cobalt and to reorganise its mining and refining sectors.

It said annual production of nickel would be raised to 213,000 tonnes by 2000 from around 177,000 tonnes in 1996 -- a bold target for any company. It aimed to lift copper output to 370,000 from 340,000 and cobalt to 4,000 tonnes from 3,151.
Norilsk spokesman Sergei Vetchinin told Reuters he thought the new production targets could be hit as early as this year.
But he did not explain how the financially-troubled group planned the healthy increases and did not know if senior managers thought that this was achievable this year.
London Metal Exchange prices for nickel have in the past swung wildly on supply disruptions at Norilsk, which is under perma-frost for much of the year.

Despite its strong producing position, Norilsk is dogged by enormous debts to regional coffers and workers. But thus far its financial crisis has not hit output or exports, company officials have said.
The Duma also urged the government to reacquire, until 2000, control over the Norilsk stake now owned by Uneximbank, which acquired the equity in a shares-for-loans auction in 1995.

Prime-Tass news agency said the nickel processing part of Norilsk's flagship combine would be closed down and that all nickel concentrates would be processed at the Nadezhdinsky plant, which has also seen output disruptions in the past.
But Vetchinin said the closing programme still had to be agreed with workers and management and many questions remained.

Plant employees, restless over unpaid wages totalling 1.3 trillion roubles ($230 million at current rates), have staged disruptions to output in the past. Norilsk's debts to regional budgets are even higher, at 1.4 trillion roubles ($250 million). ($1 = 5,662 roubles) REUTER MCW LEB
